title: The Refugee Who Invented Islamic Banking
event_summary: In 1953, Ahmad El-Naggar, an Egyptian economist who had fled Nasser's crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood, began developing the theoretical framework for interest-free banking while studying in Germany and collaborating with Pakistani scholars in Karachi. Drawing on medieval Islamic jurisprudence and German cooperative savings bank models, he designed a system of profit-sharing deposits and equity-based lending that eliminated riba (usury). His ideas first materialized in the Mit Ghamr Savings Bank in Egypt's Nile Delta in 1963, which attracted over 60,000 depositors in its first three years by offering a banking system compatible with Islamic law.
why_forgotten: El-Naggar's experiment was shut down by the Egyptian government in 1967, which absorbed the bank into the state postal system and erased its independent identity. His work was dismissed by Western economists as a quaint religious curiosity irrelevant to modern finance. Because the movement emerged from exiled dissidents operating across borders, no single nation claimed credit for it.
why_it_matters: Islamic finance today represents a $4 trillion global industry spanning 80 countries, with major Western banks operating Sharia-compliant divisions. El-Naggar's model of profit-and-loss sharing influenced alternative finance movements worldwide, including microfinance and ethical banking. His framework proved that a parallel financial system could operate at scale outside the interest-based architecture that had dominated global banking since the Renaissance.
